newsitem.title: UK: OPEC output creeps up in Oct to 25.97 mbpd - surve.
newsitem.headline: OPEC output creeps up in Oct to 25.97 mbpd - surve.

text.p: OPEC oil production crept higher in October, once again overshooting its long-ignored output ceiling but a resilient oil price seems to indicate the group is far from overproducing, analysts say.

A Reuter survey of oil analysts, industry sources and OPEC delegates on Thursday showed that the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries pumped out 25.97 million barrels per day (bpd), up from 25.86 million in September.

Quota violations by most of the 11 members meant that the cartel was nearly one million bpd over its 25.03 million bpd ceiling as a prolonged oil price rally encouraged most of them to take advantage of strong pre-winter demand.
The price of the official OPEC crude "basket", the average of prices of seven different crude grades, has been over OPEC's own target of $21 a barrel for months.

"The higher price is probably encouraging higher production but one cannot really say there is overproduction since it is being absorbed," said veteran OPEC watcher Mehdi Varzi of Kleinwort Benson in London,

OPEC and other oil production have enjoyed windfall revenues this years as Middle East tensions, strong demand and very low heating oil stocks ahead of the peak winter fuel use period have pushed prices to their highest levels in nearly six years and far beyond the most bullish forecasts.
Though the rally has cooled in the last couple weeks, analysts say prices should remain fairly strong until it becomes clear how cold the winter will be.
Varzi reckons that for every $1 a barrel gain in the price, OPEC countries make a combined $15 billion extra in export revenue.
But the group is not likely to cash in on the price bonanza by officially increasing its ceiling when ministers meet later this month in Vienna to set 1997 levels.
Most members, including influential Saudi Arabia, are not keen to open debate about market share -- always a contentious issue for OPEC.

"Any increase would be a cosmetically bad signal for the market and it would only encourage further indiscipline which will be more difficult to restrain when prices fall," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.
Venezuela continued as OPEC's biggest quota buster in October, pumping about 3.15 million bpd, well over its 2.36 million bpd quota.

Despite repeated public denials, Venezuelan oil industry officials privately confirm the high production. The head of state oil concern PDVSA, Luis Guisti, told a congressional commission in Caracas this week, output will average over 3.4 million next year.
"There is no way Venezuela will ever look back now. For all practical purposes, it is not really a member of OPEC now," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, an oil consultant at Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC).
But after repeated attempts by OPEC to cajole Venezuela to rein in output, Saudi Arabia and others seems to prefer to keep mum now and hope the market continues to absorb the extra barrels.

The three powerful Middle East Gulf members -- Saudi Arabia, UAE and to a lesser extent Kuwait -- have remained relatively restrained considering they are the only countries in the world with serious spare oil production capacity, OPEC delegates say.
"Face it, we all are over quota and all at capacity except Saudi and a couple others," said a senior delegate at a non-Gulf OPEC member.
"The key producers have been remarkably restrained but in doing so their are virtually acting as swing producers," Kleinwort's Varzi said.
OPEC heavyweight Saudi Arabia, which exports more than double the amount of oil as its nearest competitor Norway, is sitting on 2.0 million bpd of unused capacity.
Though a number of OPEC observers say the kingdom may be slightly over its longheld 8.0 million bpd quota, it is hardly flooding the market.
The Reuter survey saw Saudi wellhead production at 8.05 million bpd, steady from September, though Saudi sources said it averaged 8.022 million bpd while supply was at quota.
The survey found higher output from Iran, Nigeria, the UAE and Venezuela while production fell in Qatar because of maintenance work at the Maydan Mahzam field until early November.
Iraq's prolonged absence from world markets, following postponement of May's U.N. oil-for-food exchange, leaves tight markets without an expected 600,000 bpd of extra fourth quarter supply.
OPEC's second largest producer Iran was slightly over its 3.6 million bpd quota in October at 3.7 million.
After several years of wildly fluctuating production because of various technical and marketing constraints, Iran seems to have stabilised its flows between 3.6-3.7 million, analysts say.
The Reuter survey seeks a best estimate of wellhead flows in OPEC countries based on the views of officials, industry monitors and analysts inside and outside member countries.
OPEC quotas are based on supply to market, defined to exclude movements to, but not sales from storage.
